transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello, Mr Quist. I'm Dr Abara, one of the emergency doctors. Is it all right if your wife stays?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, please. This is Imelda.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Hello, doctor.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Can you tell me what happened today?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I was in the garden, digging, and I got this pain in my chest.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: When did it start?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: After lunch. No, before. I hadn't eaten yet. About eleven o'clock.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: It was just before eleven. I'd just put the kettle on.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay, about eleven. Can you show me where the pain was?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Here, in the middle. Like a heavy weight sitting on me.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Did it go anywhere else?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Down my left arm.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long did it last?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About half an hour. It's eased off now, but it's still there a bit. Maybe three out of ten.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Did you feel sweaty or sick with it?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Very sweaty. Not sick.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Short of breath?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A bit.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you had anything like this before?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, never.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any heart problems in the past?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. Just blood pressure. I'm on amlodipine.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What dose?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Five milligrams.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any other medicines?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Do you smoke?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, about twenty a day. I know.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Anyone in the family with heart problems?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My father had a heart attack at 52.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: And my dad had his at 60, but that's my side.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you. The paramedics gave you aspirin, 300 milligrams, I can see that on their sheet.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, they did. And a spray under my tongue.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Let me examine you. Your heart rate is 88 and regular, blood pressure 152 over 90. Your heart sounds are normal. Your chest is clear. Oxygen level is 97 percent. No swelling in your ankles.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Your ECG, the heart tracing, shows some changes. There's about a millimetre of ST depression in the leads on the left side of the chest, V4 to V6. That can be a sign the heart muscle isn't getting enough blood.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Is he having a heart attack?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: It's possible. It could be what we call an acute coronary syndrome. We've taken a blood test for troponin, which shows heart muscle damage, and we'll repeat it in a few hours.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What happens now?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'm going to start an injection called fondaparinux, 2.5 milligrams under the skin once a day, to thin the blood. You can have GTN spray if the pain comes back.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'm going to admit you under the cardiology team. They'll likely want to do an angiogram, a test to look at the heart arteries.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: We'll repeat your ECG every time you get pain, and in the meantime please tell the nurses straight away if the pain comes back or gets worse.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I will.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Thank you, doctor.

reference_note.presenting_complaint: Central chest pain starting at about 11:00 while gardening.
reference_note.history: Heavy central chest pain radiating to the left arm, lasting about 30 minutes; ongoing at 3/10. Associated sweating and mild breathlessness; no nausea. No previous similar episodes or known cardiac disease. Hypertension. Smoker, 20 per day. Father had a myocardial infarction at 52. Aspirin 300 mg and GTN given by ambulance crew.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Amlodipine 5 mg once daily. No known drug allergies.
reference_note.examination: HR 88 regular, BP 152/90, SpO2 97% on air. Heart sounds normal. Chest clear. No peripheral oedema. ECG: sinus rhythm, 1 mm ST depression in V4–V6.
reference_note.plan: Serial high-sensitivity troponin. Fondaparinux 2.5 mg subcutaneously once daily. GTN spray as required. Admit under cardiology; likely coronary angiography. Repeat ECG with any further pain.
reference_note.safety_netting: Asked to report recurrent or worsening pain to nursing staff immediately.
